comparison: Perfect agreement on behavioral findings (C37-C41). Both evaluations find the RT facilitation data compelling and well-supported with appropriate statistical analyses. OpenEval emphasizes the statistical rigor (repeated measures ANOVA, Bayesian analysis), while peer reviewers highlight the overall quality of experimental design. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Strong agreement on core neural findings (C48-C52). Both evaluations affirm the broad, stimulus-unspecific suppression in EVC. OpenEval notes the surprising discrepancy between neural breadth and behavioral specificity, while peer reviewers accept the findings without questioning this discrepancy. Both find the evidence robust across all stimulus types.

Strong agreement on proactive suppression via omission trials (C33, C54-C56, C89-C90). Both evaluations view this as a key contribution. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of confound controls (C118-C121), while peer reviewers universally highlight the proactive interpretation as addressing theoretical debates. Both accept the evidence without challenge.

Strong agreement on implicit learning evidence (C61-C65, C95-C97). OpenEval emphasizes the converging lines of evidence and appropriate use of Bayesian statistics for null effects. Peer Reviewer 3 specifically praises the 'careful application of follow-up analyses to rule out alternative, strategy-based accounts.' Both evaluations fully support the implicit learning interpretation.

Perfect agreement on robustness controls (C67-C70). Both evaluations affirm these control analyses validate the main findings. OpenEval notes they demonstrate results are not artifacts of analysis parameters. Peer Reviewer 3 specifically praises 'tests of the robustness of the findings to detailed analysis parameters such as ROI size.' Both find these controls strengthen confidence in primary findings.

Agreement on main findings summary (C4-C9, C31-C32 overlap with C4-C5, C31, C48-C52). Both evaluations support the characterization of suppression as spatially specific yet broad and stimulus-unspecific. OpenEval explicitly connects these summary claims to underlying data, while peer reviewers affirm the overall pattern. Both accept the inference that suppression precedes stimulus identification.

Partial overlap on stimulus-unspecific suppression characterization (C6-C9, C32). Both evaluations strongly support these claims. Peer reviewers consistently affirmed suppression occurs 'in response to all stimuli' across all three reviewers. OpenEval emphasizes the logical inference that suppression precedes identification. Complete agreement on this aspect of the findings.

Strong agreement on theoretical interpretation and integration (C71, C73-C74, C82, C124, C130-C131). Both evaluations endorse the overall framework and contextualization within prior work. OpenEval finds the interpretation well-supported and appropriately cited. Peer reviewers praise the study as addressing 'theoretical debates' and providing 'an advance over previous studies.' Both accept the multifaceted characterization of distractor suppression.

Divergent evaluation of speculative claims (C76-C78, C80, C125). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative and not directly tested, requiring future work on downstream processing. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the overall theoretical framework without distinguishing speculative elements. OpenEval is more cautious about claims lacking direct empirical support.

Agreement on stimulus type effects (C45-C46). Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval notes the interpretation as reasonable inference rather than directly tested, with small but reliable effect sizes. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as consistent with established literature without raising concerns. Both find the evidence adequate.

Divergent evaluation of V1/V2 exploratory findings (C113-C115). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing substantial limitations (lack of functional retinotopy, volumetric space) and characterizing findings as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Peer Reviewer 3 rates as SUPPORTED, noting these analyses 'enhance' main findings. OpenEval is more cautious about methodological limitations affecting reliability.

Partial overlap on behavioral control analyses (C59-C60). Both evaluations support the evidence that neural suppression does not impair target processing. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of multiple converging lines of evidence. Peer Reviewer 3 endorses the 'careful application of follow-up analyses.' Both accept the dissociation between neural and behavioral effects.

OpenEval evaluated claims ruling out repetition suppression (C100-C106) as SUPPORTED, noting multiple lines of evidence and sound logic. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addressed these alternative explanations, though they were implicitly accepted as part of the overall interpretation.

OpenEval evaluated claim about statistical learning vs. priming (C108) as UNCERTAIN due to acknowledged underpowering and limitations. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addressed this distinction, suggesting peer reviewers did not scrutinize this specific alternative explanation.

OpenEval evaluated claims about feedback vs. local storage mechanisms (C109-C112) as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative hypotheses not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation addressed these mechanistic questions, suggesting peer reviewers focused on empirical findings rather than mechanistic speculation.

OpenEval evaluated methodological reporting claims (C132-C139) as SUPPORTED, affirming sample size justification, exclusion criteria, and ethical procedures. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly assessed these methodological details, though they were implicitly accepted through overall approval.

OpenEval evaluated arguments addressing omission trial confounds (C118-C121) as SUPPORTED, finding the logic sound and strengthening the proactive interpretation. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addressed these methodological concerns, though peer reviewers universally accepted the proactive interpretation without raising these potential confounds.

OpenEval evaluated claims about temporal resolution limitations (C122-C123) as SUPPORTED, finding the qualification appropriate and reasoning sound. No corresponding peer review evaluation addressed this methodological limitation, suggesting peer reviewers did not scrutinize temporal resolution constraints on the proactive interpretation.
